title: The History of Women’s Football
author: Latoyah Innerarity
source: FFT Tutoring with the Lightning Squad (tutoring.fft.org.uk), screenshots supplied 6 Oct 2026

pages.heading: The Final
pages.text: It was a nail-biting match. The 2022 Women’s European Championship final between England and Germany had reached its second half and neither team had scored. With 80,000 fans packed into Wembley stadium and millions watching at home, the stakes were high. Finally, 20 minutes into the second half, England’s Ella Toone scored, sending the crowd into a frenzy of cheers. 17 minutes later Germany silenced the crowd by scoring to level the match at 1 - 1. After some tense near misses by both teams, it was still neck and neck with extra time ticking towards an end. With the prospect of penalty kicks looming, it was Chloe Kelly who, with minutes to spare, scored England’s winning goal.

Finally, 20 minutes into the second half, England’s Ella Toone scored, sending the crowd into a frenzy of cheers. 17 minutes later Germany silenced the crowd by scoring to level the match at 1 - 1.

After some tense near misses by both teams, it was still neck and neck with extra time ticking towards an end. With the prospect of penalty kicks looming, it was Chloe Kelly who, with minutes to spare, scored England’s winning goal.

pages.heading: The Lionesses
pages.text: For England, whose last major tournament win was the men’s 1966 World Cup, it was a triumphant end to 56 disappointing years of defeat. Football had finally made its way home, bringing with it a new group of sport sensations – The Lionesses – a variation on the men’s team name: The Three Lions. But, before their historic win against Germany, there was little known about the Lionesses and women’s football in general. Mostly considered a man’s game, women’s football has struggled to achieve the same recognition and respect. Let’s explore how, after more than a century of setbacks, bans and discrimination, the girls and women kicked, dribbled and scored their way into the hearts of fans across the country.

Let’s explore how, after more than a century of setbacks, bans and discrimination, the girls and women kicked, dribbled and scored their way into the hearts of fans across the country.

pages.heading: The First Match
pages.text: There is evidence that women have played football for centuries, but the first official match took place in North London, 1895. This was after the launch of the British Ladies Football Club by Nettie Honeyball, although it’s widely believed she made this name up! She managed to convince wealthy suffragette Lady Florence Dixie to finance and help manage the club with her. Honeyball and Dixie placed an advert in a magazine asking women to join the team and promised a share of any profits they made. Around 30 young women responded and a few men, for a joke! The women who applied were inexperienced but they had a love for the game and enthusiastically attended twice weekly training sessions. Eventually they were divided into north and south teams that would play against each other. This first football match was seen by the public, as something new, strange and maybe even a little funny and was attended by around 11,000 paying spectators.

pages.heading: A Bigger Idea
pages.text: Whilst a love of football inspired Ms Honeyball and Lady Dixie to start the British Ladies Football Association, they had an even bigger idea in mind - to show men that women weren’t ‘useless’. They wanted to challenge outdated views about the role of women in society and further the cause for women’s equality. They saw no better way to achieve this than with football - the game at the heart of the nation. The timing was especially perfect as the Industrial Revolution was taking place and many women were entering the workforce for the first time. Employment gave women a visibility and independence they hadn’t experienced before and allowed them to challenge the stereotype that they were only suited for domestic duties like cooking and cleaning.

pages.heading: Mocked by the Press
pages.text: The British Ladies Football Association showed that women had diverse skills and also challenged ideas on how ladies should exercise and the kind of sports suitable for them, as at the time women playing contact sports was considered unladylike. The press, however, belittled the players, with one bestselling newspaper printing a mocking cartoon of the ladies using half-time to style their hair and the male spectators only being interested in the good-looking players. Despite being ridiculed, the football team did have some success when they toured and played matches across the country. Their success was unfortunately short lived, as the following year, due to financial difficulties, the British Ladies Football Club was forced to shut down.

pages.heading: Women at War
pages.text: For many years women’s football was virtually invisible until the outbreak of the first world war where it gained prominence, once again. With the majority of men off fighting in the war, women were needed more than ever to take on male jobs. The industries they worked in varied - some were railway guards, postal workers and bank tellers, but mostly they filled the vacancies in factories that made weapons and ammunition. Not only were these factories damp and dirty, but the exposure to toxic chemicals also made them incredibly dangerous to work in.

pages.heading: Factory Teams
pages.text: The government and factory bosses encouraged team sports to boost health, productivity and well-being, particularly as many of the women had lost brothers, fathers and husbands in the war. The women began playing football during their tea and lunch breaks and eventually many factories established their own teams. The most successful of these factory teams was Dick, Kerr Ladies F.C. Dick, Kerr was a manufacturer of trains and tramcars, and their ladies football team played in over 800 games during a 50 year period and won 746! They also produced the country’s best ever scorer, Lily Parr who scored 900 goals during her 30-year career and was the first female player to be featured in the National Football Museum Hall of Fame.

pages.heading: Dick, Kerr Ladies
pages.text: Dick, Kerr F.C. started like other factory teams, by playing friendly matches during their breaks. However, as their skills developed, they were noticed by factory worker, Alfred Frankland, who would watch them play from his office window. Frankland was known for his skill with business and marketing and he went on to become the team’s first manager. Their first official match was a Christmas day charity game that drew over 10,000 spectators and raised £600 (equivalent to around £43,000 today) for injured soldiers! The popularity of the Dick, Kerr F.C. continued to grow, perhaps, in part, because the men’s leagues were suspended during the war. They frequently toured the country raising money for hospitals and injured service men. In total, they raised the equivalent of 2 million pounds during the war years.

pages.heading: After the War
pages.text: After the war many factories closed, and women were pushed back into domestic roles or re-trained as nurses or bus conductors. Women’s football, however, continued to flourish, particularly Dick, Kerr F.C. who were now celebrities. Their 1920 Boxing Day match in Liverpool was said to have generated more income, at the time, than any other football game in history, making £3,000 (approx. £140,000 today) from 53,000 paying spectators. The Football Association (FA) and government noticed the growing popularity of women’s football and became concerned about how profits were being spent. With the war over, the women were now using profits to support political and working class causes the government didn’t approve of. They were also concerned the women were taking money and fans away from the men’s football league, particularly as the FA had recently spent a lot of money expanding it.

pages.heading: The Ban
pages.text: Initially, the FA and government began making it difficult for women to play football. For example, they had to submit account statements after every match and they couldn’t play without prior permission from the FA. Eventually, in 1921 they were banned all together, with the excuse that football was unsuitable for women and could prevent them from becoming pregnant. Of course, women couldn’t be stopped from playing entirely but they were banned from using professional FA grounds, clubs and referees. This meant women were forced to play football in parks or small rugby grounds but without the capacity stadiums offered, public interest in the sport declined.

pages.heading: The Swinging Sixties
pages.text: The ban remained in place for 50 years during which time World War II began and ended. During this time, Dick, Kerr F.C. went to America, where they had some success playing against men, as the country had few women’s teams. It wasn’t until what’s commonly known as the ‘Swinging Sixties’ that women’s football, in England, finally began to rise from the ashes. The Swinging Sixties was a decade of change. Propelled by the end of post-war poverty and new economic prosperity, society became less rigid. Out went traditional ways of doing things and in came modern ways of thinking.

pages.heading: A Revival
pages.text: In 1964, the Labour party won the general election, ending 13 years of Conservative rule. Labour came to power with promises of greater equality and it was amongst this optimistic atmosphere that women’s football began experiencing a revival. In 1969, forty-four British women’s teams came together to form the Women’s Football Association (WFA). They initially tried pressurising the FA to lift the ban, but were met with no success. Undeterred, they hosted tournaments between the female teams in local fields. Eventually, they toured the country playing against willing men’s teams, which local newspapers reported on favourably. Realising that women’s football was, once again, gaining energy, the FA decided to lift the ban in 1971, with the idea they could control and manage its growth.

Realising that women’s football was, once again, gaining energy, the FA decided to lift the ban in 1971, with the idea they could control and manage its growth.

pages.heading: Playing Abroad
pages.text: However, the FA’s management of women’s football was poor, as they refused to offer financial support and side-lined the WFA who they had agreed to work with. Yes, the ban had been lifted but without the FA’s genuine desire to embrace women’s football, its development was minimal. Many female footballers decided to play in other countries such as Italy, where the women’s league was better established. In these countries, women’s football was popular and making a lot of money. This attracted the attention of FIFA (the global football governing body) and it now looked as though international tournaments could be in the future of women’s football.

pages.heading: World Cups and Leagues
pages.text: FIFA introduced the Women’s World Cup in 1991. Held in China, this featured 12 teams from 6 continents, with the USA winning the title against Norway. Across the tournament an impressive half a million fans came to watch which helped raise the profile of women’s football and inspired a new generation of female footballers. In 2005, England hosted the UEFA Women’s Euro which broke records for crowd attendance and TV audiences. Then came the Women’s Super League in 2011, which replaced the Women’s Premier League as the highest level of competition in England.

pages.heading: A Legacy
pages.text: With increased investment, media coverage and participation, women’s football was becoming unstoppable and paved the way for landmark victories like ’the Lionesses victory at the 2022 Euros and their finals appearance’: at the Women’s World Cup in 2023. “After the Euros and World Cup, we wanted to create a legacy,” England (Lioness) defender Lucy Bronze said in an interview. The Lionesses and the women who came before them have done just that, showing the entire world that anything boys can do, girls can too.

glossary.tense: Nervous and worried, because you don’t know what will happen.
glossary.suffragette: A woman who campaigned for women to have the right to vote, in the early 1900s.
glossary.ridiculed: Made fun of in an unkind way.
glossary.vacancies: Jobs that are empty and need someone to do them.
glossary.prosperity: Having plenty of money and doing well.
glossary.optimistic: Hopeful that things will turn out well.
